content: Catechins are polyphenolic antioxidant compounds classified as flavonoids, specifically flavan-3-ols. These compounds are found in various plant species, but the primary dietary source for humans is tea derived from the tea plant, Camellia sinensis. Catechin, epicatechin, gallocatechin, epigallocatechin, and their gallate derivatives are structurally related epimers. Among these, (-)-epicatechin and (+)-catechin are the most commonly occurring optical isomers in nature. Catechin was originally isolated from the plant extract catechu, which is the source of its name. When catechin is heated beyond its decomposition point, it releases pyrocatechol, which explains the shared etymology of these compounds. Epigallocatechin and gallocatechin differ from epicatechin and catechin, respectively, by the presence of an additional phenolic hydroxyl group, analogous to the structural difference between pyrogallol and pyrocatechol. Catechin gallates, such as epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG), are esters of catechins with gallic acid, with EGCG being the most abundant catechin in tea. Catechins make up approximately 25% of the dry weight of fresh tea leaves, although their total content can vary significantly depending on factors such as clonal variation, growing location, seasonal and light conditions, and altitude. They are present in nearly all teas made from Camellia sinensis, including white tea, green tea, black tea, and oolong tea. Catechins are also found in other dietary sources such as chocolate, fruits, vegetables, and wine, as well as in many other plant species. The health benefits of catechins have been extensively studied in both humans and animal models. In animal studies, catechins have been shown to reduce atherosclerotic plaque formation. In vitro studies have demonstrated their potential to reduce carcinogenesis. Numerous health benefits have been attributed to the catechin content in various foods and beverages. According to Dr. Norman Hollenberg, a professor of medicine at Harvard Medical School, epicatechin may reduce the risk of four major health conditions: stroke, heart failure, cancer, and diabetes. His research on the Kuna people of Panama, who consume up to 40 cups of cocoa per week, revealed that the prevalence of these big four diseases is less than 10% among this population. Additionally, epigallocatechin-3-gallate (EGCG) has been identified as a potent antioxidant that helps protect the skin from damage caused by UV radiation and may reduce the risk of tumor formation.
